questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Who sets the mode of appointing electors
questions.learningObjective: Identify the body that fixes the time, place, and manner of choosing electors

stimulus.body: Our consultant notes that a recent change in how the state chooses its presidential electors was made by the state legislature, not by the federal government or the city. I want the file to reflect that the legislature can set the time, place, and manner of choosing electors.

questions.stem: According to the memo, which body has the authority to set the manner of choosing electors in the state?

options.text: The state legislature, which may fix the time, place, and manner of appointing the electors.
The city council, which controls elections conducted within municipal boundaries.
options.misconception: assumes local officials set the method of appointment

options.text: Congress, which regulates the counting of electoral votes in every state.
options.misconception: assumes Congress controls how electors are chosen

options.text: The political party, which nominates electors and therefore determines the method.
options.misconception: assumes a party controls the legal method of selection

questions.explanation: Article II leaves the time, place, and manner of appointing electors to the state legislature. Congress may regulate the counting of votes but not the state's method of choosing electors.
questions.hint: Ask which level of government holds this power.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Consent required for an agreement among states
questions.learningObjective: Calculate the number of approvals required before an interstate agreement is submitted
questions.stem: The planner's memo explains that an agreement among states requires the consent of Congress, and that a council of seven state delegations must approve the request first. Five delegations have approved. How many more approvals are needed?
questions.explanation: Consent from Congress is required before the agreement binds the states, and the memo's precondition requires all seven delegations. With five approvals, two more delegations must approve.
questions.hint: Subtract approvals given from the number required.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Whether a state may bind its electors by law
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a state cannot instruct its electors how to vote
questions.stem: A planner asks why a state law directing presidential electors to vote for whichever candidate carries the state cannot be sustained.

options.text: Because electors are federal officers, so their selection and their votes are governed only by federal law.
options.misconception: treats electors as federal rather than state officers

options.text: Because a state may regulate how electors are chosen, but may not bind the electors to a candidate.
Because the popular vote is the only lawful basis on which a state may allocate its electors.
options.misconception: assumes states must allocate electors by popular vote

options.text: Because a state may not regulate the conduct of a presidential election at all.
options.misconception: assumes states may not regulate elections at all

questions.explanation: A state may regulate the time, place, and manner of choosing electors, but it may not enact a pledge telling electors how to vote. Such a law intrudes on the electors' lawful discretion.
questions.hint: Ask what the state may control about electors.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: A popular-vote winner who loses the presidency
questions.learningObjective: State what the Constitution provides about the national popular vote
questions.stem: A planner notes that a candidate won the national popular vote but lost the presidency, and asks what the Constitution provides about that outcome.

options.text: The Constitution provides that the candidate with the most popular votes nationwide shall become president.
options.misconception: believes a national popular vote determines the presidency

options.text: The Constitution provides that Congress must reopen the count and select the popular-vote winner.
options.misconception: invents a congressional tie-breaking role that does not exist

options.text: The Constitution has no national popular vote rule, so the outcome follows from the state electoral system.
The Constitution provides that the loser must be seated once a majority of electors certify the count.
options.misconception: confuses certification of the count with the constitutional outcome

questions.explanation: The Constitution creates a state-based system of electors, so a candidate who wins the national popular vote can lose the presidency. Nothing in the text requires a national popular vote to control the result.
questions.hint: Ask whether the Constitution mentions such a vote.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Margins and block allocation
questions.learningObjective: Calculate the electoral votes a candidate receives under a split allocation method
questions.stem: A planning model for the memo uses a state with twelve electoral votes, of which eight are awarded by congressional district and four as a statewide block. A candidate wins three of the eight districts and also carries the statewide vote. How many electoral votes does the candidate receive?
questions.explanation: The candidate takes one elector for each of the three districts won and the four electors awarded by the statewide contest, so three plus four gives seven electoral votes. The entitlement of twelve is unchanged by the method.
questions.hint: Add the district wins to the statewide electors.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: The single-member bias
questions.learningObjective: Explain why single-member districts can overstate a party's vote share
questions.stem: A planner reviews a study showing that a party with 58 percent of the vote won only 45 percent of single-member seats, and asks why that happens.

options.text: Because single-member districts require a runoff whenever no candidate reaches 50 percent of the vote.
options.misconception: confuses single-member districts with majority runoffs

options.text: Because voters in single-member districts may not vote for candidates of their own party alone.
options.misconception: invents a ballot restriction to explain seat totals

options.text: Because each single-member district is required to contain an equal share of each party's voters.
options.misconception: describes a proportional allocation rule that districts do not use

options.text: Because one winner is chosen by plurality, which over-rewards a party whose votes are efficiently packed.

questions.explanation: Single-member districts award each seat to one plurality winner, so a party that packs supporters efficiently can win seats out of proportion to its vote share. That is the single-member bias.
questions.hint: Think about plurality winners in one-member districts.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Plurality and majority rules compared
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish a plurality rule from a majority rule in a single-member contest

stimulus.body: Our district plan will use single-member contests in most wards. The consultant asks whether we should require a majority of the vote for a win and, if not, how the rule should be described in the plan's preamble.

questions.stem: How does the plurality rule used in a single-member district differ from a majority rule in the memo's situation?

options.text: A plurality rule requires a runoff whenever the top candidate falls short of 50 percent of the vote.
options.misconception: conflates plurality with a majority requirement

options.text: Plurality lets the top candidate win with less than half, while a majority rule requires more than half.
Both rules require a majority of the vote, but the majority rule adds a runoff if no one reaches it.
options.misconception: assumes a plurality rule also demands a majority

options.text: A majority rule is the same as plurality in a single-member district, since only one seat is contested.
options.misconception: claims the two rules are interchangeable

questions.explanation: Plurality awards the seat to the candidate with the most votes even if that is under half, the rule used in nearly every single-member district. A majority rule requires more than half and often a runoff.
questions.hint: Ask how many votes each rule demands of the winner.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: A three-way district contest
questions.learningObjective: Calculate the margin between the leading candidates in a three-way contest
questions.stem: A planner's memo records a three-way district contest in which one candidate has 44 percent of the vote, a second has 33 percent, and a third has 23 percent. How many percentage points separate the two leading candidates?
questions.explanation: The two leaders stand at 44 and 33 percent, so the gap between them is 11 percentage points. The third candidate at 23 percent trails the leader and does not change the plurality ranking.
questions.hint: Subtract the second-place share from the first-place share.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: How a boundary change moves a seat
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a congressional seat can move from one state to another
questions.stem: A planner learns that a border shift following the census moved a congressional seat from one state to a neighboring state, and asks why the seat can move at all.

options.text: Because the number of representatives a state receives is recalculated from its population after each census.
Because a state legislature may transfer representatives to another state with the consent of Congress.
options.misconception: believes seats can be traded between states

options.text: Because every boundary change automatically shifts one seat out of each neighboring state.
options.misconception: assumes automatic seat transfers between neighboring states

options.text: Because the number of seats is set by the number of cities in each state rather than by population.
options.misconception: claims seats are allocated by number of cities

questions.explanation: Seats follow population, which is recounted each census, so a state that gains residents can gain a seat while a losing state loses one. The shift follows from the count, not from any transfer.
questions.hint: Ask what determines how many representatives a state has.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: A line drawn by race and a line drawn by party
questions.learningObjective: Compare the review applied to racial and partisan districting lines
questions.stem: A planner compares two districting proposals: one drawn so that a racial group is concentrated in two districts, and one drawn to advantage a party in several districts.

options.text: Both are subject to strict scrutiny, because both involve politically motivated line drawing.
options.misconception: applies strict scrutiny to any politically drawn line

options.text: Neither is subject to heightened review, because line drawing is a legislative choice made by elected officials.
options.misconception: treats all districting as free from constitutional review

options.text: The partisan proposal is reviewed strictly, while the racial proposal is reviewed under rational basis.
options.misconception: reverses the scrutiny applied to race and party

options.text: A line drawn by race is reviewed strictly, while a line drawn for partisan advantage is treated differently.

questions.explanation: A districting drawn on racial lines must satisfy strict scrutiny because race is a suspect classification, while partisan line drawing is generally not a federal constitutional violation, though states may regulate it by statute.
questions.hint: Ask which line rests on a suspect classification.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Who sets the mode of appointing electors
questions.learningObjective: Calculate the number of electors a state receives from its congressional delegation
questions.stem: A planner's memo models a hypothetical state with 2 senators and 17 members of Congress and asks how many presidential electors that state would have.
questions.explanation: Every state receives electors equal to its total congressional delegation, so two senators plus seventeen representatives produce nineteen electors. The model counts electors, not members of Congress.
questions.hint: Add the senators to the representatives.

questions.topic: Consent required for an agreement among states
questions.learningObjective: Identify the consent required before an interstate agreement becomes binding
questions.stem: A planner wants two neighboring cities to share a transit fare system, and asks what the cities must obtain before their agreement can be binding.

options.text: Approval from their two city councils, and nothing more, because cities are political subdivisions.
options.misconception: assumes local approval alone settles the question

options.text: A referendum of the voters in both cities, since an agreement affects the public fisc.
options.misconception: assumes a popular vote is the required federal step

options.text: The consent of Congress, because states cannot enter agreements without it.
A decision of the President, which must approve interstate agreements on transit.
options.misconception: assigns the approval to the executive branch

questions.explanation: Article I provides that no state may enter into an agreement with another state without the consent of Congress. Arrangements wholly within one state are handled under state law instead.
questions.hint: Ask what the Constitution requires before states combine.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Whether a state may bind its electors by law
questions.learningObjective: Assess a proposed state pledge of electors for legal validity

stimulus.body: The bill would require every presidential elector in the state to vote for the candidate who receives the greatest number of votes in the state. A committee note observes that the state already sets the time, place, and manner of the election and asks whether the bill adds anything permissible.

questions.stem: Under the bill summary's reasoning, how should the committee describe the proposed pledge of electors?

options.text: As a harmless addition, because the state already controls how electors are appointed.
options.misconception: assumes appointment power extends to electors' votes

options.text: As impermissible, because a state may not bind its electors by law to a candidate.
As a constitutional improvement, because voters should control the electors' votes.
options.misconception: assumes a state may direct electors' votes

options.text: As a matter for the local council, because electors are chosen in the district where they serve.
options.misconception: treats elector selection as a local administrative matter

questions.explanation: The state may set the time, place, and manner of choosing electors, but a pledge that dictates their votes is not part of that authority. Courts have treated such pledges as unconstitutional.
questions.hint: Ask whether appointment power covers the votes.

questions.learningObjective: Calculate the electoral vote shortfall of a popular-vote winner
questions.stem: A planner's memo notes that a candidate who won the national popular vote carried 268 electoral votes and asks how many more electoral votes would have been needed to reach 270.
questions.explanation: A candidate needs 270 electoral votes to win, so a total of 268 falls two votes short. The example shows how a large popular-vote margin can coexist with a shortfall in the electoral count.
questions.hint: Subtract the votes held from the total required.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Margins and block allocation
questions.learningObjective: Explain how switching allocation methods can change an electoral outcome
questions.stem: A planner asks why a state that switches from awarding electors in one statewide block to awarding them by congressional district can change the electoral outcome even when the vote totals are unchanged.

options.text: Because district-by-district wins change which candidate carries each district, and small differences in margin can add or remove electors.
Because the district method changes the total number of electors the state is entitled to.
options.misconception: assumes the method changes the state's entitlement

options.text: Because voters in a district method are voting on electors rather than on candidates.
options.misconception: confuses the unit of voting under each method

options.text: Because a district method removes the popular vote from the state entirely.
options.misconception: believes the popular vote disappears in a district method

questions.explanation: Under the district method each district's winner takes one elector, so a candidate's statewide margin becomes separate district contests, and small differences can swing electors. The state's entitlement is unchanged.
questions.hint: Ask how the method changes the unit of winning.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: The single-member bias
questions.learningObjective: Explain how proportional allocation reduces the single-member bias
questions.stem: A planner considers replacing two single-member council districts with a multi-member district allocated by proportional vote, and asks what difference that would make.

options.text: It would make each council member responsible to a smaller group of voters than before.
options.misconception: assumes proportional districts shrink each member's constituency

options.text: It would guarantee that the party with the most votes wins a majority of the seats.
options.misconception: assumes proportional allocation always yields a majority

options.text: It would remove the need for voters to choose among several named candidates in a contest.
options.misconception: assumes multi-member districts feature no candidate choice

options.text: It would reduce the single-member bias, because proportional allocation can match seats to votes more closely.

questions.explanation: Proportional allocation lets a party win roughly the share of seats its votes support, so a party with 45 percent of the vote is not shut out. That is the opposite of the single-member bias.
questions.hint: Ask how the seat-vote relationship changes with allocation.

questions.topic: Plurality and majority rules compared
questions.learningObjective: Compare the vote shares of plurality and majority winners
questions.stem: A planner's memo compares two single-member contests. In the first, the winner holds 38 percent of the vote; in the second, the winner holds 54 percent. By how many percentage points does the second winner's share exceed the first winner's share?
questions.explanation: The first contest is a plurality win well under half, while the second clears the majority threshold. The gap between the two winners' shares is 54 minus 38, or 16 percentage points.
questions.hint: Subtract the smaller percentage from the larger.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: A three-way district contest
questions.learningObjective: Explain the effect of a third candidate on a plurality contest
questions.stem: A planner watches a council district race in which two major candidates split the vote and a third draws about a fifth, and asks what the third candidate's effect is.

options.text: The third candidate's votes are excluded from the total because a district has only one seat.
options.misconception: assumes minor-candidate votes are discarded

options.text: The third candidate must receive a majority of the district's votes to have any effect.
options.misconception: assumes a majority is required for a minor candidate

options.text: The third candidate can draw support away from a major candidate and change which one wins the seat.
The third candidate must withdraw before the election to have any chance of winning.
options.misconception: believes withdrawal is a precondition to any effect

questions.explanation: In a plurality contest a third candidate can pull votes from one of the two front runners, and the seat can flip accordingly. The votes are counted, and no majority is required for a candidate to matter.
questions.hint: Ask how a third candidate can shift the top two.

questions.topic: How a boundary change moves a seat
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish the effect of a ward boundary change on a city's seat totals

stimulus.body: The bulletin reports that a redistricting plan shifted the boundary of one council ward, moving about 900 registered voters from the northern part of the city into the neighboring ward, and asks whether the number of council seats available to the city changes.

questions.stem: According to the bulletin, what is the effect of moving those voters between two wards of the same city?

options.text: The city's total number of council seats changes, because the voters move to another jurisdiction.
options.misconception: confuses a ward line change with a change in entitlement

options.text: The seat totals of the two wards change, but the city's overall number of seats does not.
Nothing changes, because a boundary has no effect once voters are assigned to their precincts.
options.misconception: assumes boundaries do not affect seat totals

options.text: The number of seats changes only after the next census, when the new boundaries are counted.
options.misconception: assumes seat totals wait for the census to change

questions.explanation: A boundary change inside a city redistributes residents among that city's existing wards, changing which voters elect which council members. The city's total number of seats is fixed by its population.
questions.hint: Distinguish a city's seat total from a ward's share.

questions.explanation: The first plan splits the ten seats evenly at five each, while the second gives the advantaged party six, which is one more than the five it held before. The comparison shows what a partisan line can shift.

questions.stem: A planner asks why Congress is not allowed to set how the states choose their presidential electors.

options.text: Because the Constitution assigns that function to the state legislatures, and Congress may not displace it.
Because Congress may regulate only the counting of votes, never the selection of electors.
options.misconception: treats counting rules as the only federal power

options.text: Because the states' elector selection is a matter of state constitutional law rather than federal law.
options.misconception: removes the federal constitutional basis for the rule

options.text: Because electors are chosen by popular vote in every state, so the method question is settled already.
options.misconception: assumes every state chooses electors by popular vote

questions.explanation: Article II gives the state legislatures the power to set the manner of appointing electors, and Congress cannot remove that assignment. Congress retains authority over counting and certifying votes.

options.misconception: assumes gubernatorial approval substitutes for federal consent

options.text: A certification by the President, which has long overseen interstate transport agreements.
options.misconception: invents an executive certification requirement

options.text: Publication in a federal register, which gives the agreement notice and effect.
options.misconception: treats publication as the source of the agreement's force

options.text: The consent of Congress, which the states must obtain before agreeing among themselves.

questions.explanation: Article I provides that no state may enter into an agreement or alliance with another state without the consent of Congress. That consent is the condition that makes an interstate compact effective.

questions.stem: A planner asks how the country could move toward a system in which the national popular vote decides the presidency.

options.text: By congressional resolution alone, since Congress already controls the counting of electoral votes.
options.misconception: believes a resolution can redesign the electoral system alone

options.text: By a decision of the President, which could appoint electors in any state.
options.misconception: assumes the President can appoint electors directly

options.text: The two methods convert the same vote totals into different seat and block wins, so the outcome can differ.
The statewide block method counts absentee ballots more generously than the district method does.

options.text: The district method applies a majority rule, so a plurality leader can lose under it.
options.misconception: assumes the district method imposes a majority requirement

questions.explanation: The same statewide vote total produces one block winner under the whole-state method and a set of district winners under the district method, and the electors those wins generate can differ. Entitlement does not change.

Plurality rules count each district's votes separately, so a party's national total is irrelevant.

options.misconception: describes a vote weighting the plurality rule does not use

questions.topic: A three-way district contest
questions.learningObjective: State how a plurality rule resolves a contest with no majority
questions.stem: A planner reviews a three-way council contest in which no candidate reaches half the vote, and asks how the winner is determined under the plan's rule.

options.text: A runoff is held between the two leading candidates, and the runoff decides the seat.
options.misconception: assumes a runoff is required in a plurality contest

options.text: The seat is awarded to the candidate with the most votes, but only if that candidate has a majority.
options.misconception: combines plurality with a majority condition

options.text: The seat is split among the three candidates in proportion to their shares of the vote.
options.misconception: assumes a council seat can be split three ways

options.text: The candidate with the most votes wins the seat outright, even without a majority of the vote.

questions.explanation: A single-member district is decided by plurality, so in a three-way contest the leading candidate takes the seat even with less than half the vote. Only a rule requiring a majority would send such a contest to a runoff.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: How a boundary change moves a seat
questions.learningObjective: Calculate a district's population after a boundary adjustment
questions.stem: The council memo records that a district must contain 50,000 residents, that the current district holds 50,900, and that a boundary change would move 900 residents out. What would the district's population be after the change?
questions.explanation: Moving 900 residents out of a district of 50,900 leaves exactly 50,000, which is the target population for the plan. The change brings the district into compliance without moving anyone into it.
questions.hint: Subtract the movers from the current population.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: A line drawn by race and a line drawn by party
questions.learningObjective: Identify the standard of review for a district drawn on racial lines
questions.stem: A planner's council debates a proposal to draw a district so that a racial group is concentrated, and asks what legal standard a court would apply.

options.text: Rational basis, because a district is a legislative rather than a constitutional question.
options.misconception: treats racial districting as a low-review legislative choice

options.text: Intermediate scrutiny, because the rule affects political participation rather than rights.
options.misconception: places racial districting in the middle tier

options.text: Strict scrutiny, because a line drawn on racial lines rests on a suspect classification.
No standard, because the plan is approved by elected officials acting for the state.
options.misconception: treats official approval as immunity from review

questions.explanation: A districting drawn on racial lines is reviewed under strict scrutiny, because race is a suspect classification, and such plans rarely satisfy it. Official approval does not change the standard.
questions.hint: Ask which classification the line rests on.
